extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, critics, and students of drama/aesthetics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating and evaluating dramatic (especially tragic) works and aesthetic judgment: how beauty is produced, the moral/social role of the stage, and the conditions under which tragic pity produces aesthetic pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty as harmony between spirit and sense
rubrics_metrics.description: "Beauty results from the harmony between spirit and sense; it addresses all the faculties of man, and can only be appreciated if a man employs fully all his strength."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The spectator/reader must bring 'an open sense, a broad heart, a spirit full of freshness.' Avoid abstraction, narrow formulas, or over-application that enervate appreciation. Anti-pattern: works that only serve 'a material for the senses' to 'suspend, thought' rather than quicken it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full engagement of faculties required for sound aesthetic judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic appreciation requires that 'all a man's nature must be on the alert' and not 'divided by abstraction, narrowed by formulas, enervated by application.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and critics should aim for work that invites complete mental and emotional involvement; beware producing or evaluating art while fatigued or merely seeking passive enjoyment (e.g., audiences 'satiated with sensual pleasure' or 'exhausted man of business').

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of specialized/technical critics on matters of taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical critics 'can only devise a technical judgment, and not an aesthetical one, embracing the whole work, in which feeling should decide.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical, overly specialized commentary is useful for details but should not substitute for holistic aesthetic judgment. Recommendation: technical critics 'keep to technicalities' and avoid pronouncing universal aesthetic laws based on limited aptitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry must balance recreation and moral ennobling
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry's recreation is often conceived 'in too restricted a manner' (mere sensuous want) but 'too much scope' is also given to pure ideal/moral ennobling; both extremes are objectionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid poems that are only sensuous recreation or only didactic moralizing. The poet's aim should be to 'free human nature from accidental hinderances, without destroying the essential ideal of our humanity.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hyperphysical exaggeration and arbitrary idealism
rubrics_metrics.description: If the poet 'seeking pure form he may easily lose himself in arbitrary and baseless conceptions' and 'Reason will abstract itself too much from experience.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not construct ideals so abstract they cannot be realized or enacted within human limits. Anti-pattern: strictly didactic works that ignore lived experience and human practicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal judge: active but not slavish; idealizing but not dreamy
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek 'a class of mind at once active, but not slavishly so, and idealizing, but not dreamy; uniting the reality of life within as few limits as possible.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The intended audience/judge for true aesthetic standards is one that balances engagement with contemplative insight; poets should aim their work at such receptivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage as a moral institution and educational instrument
rubrics_metrics.description: The stage serves as a 'bridge' between senses and thought, giving 'nourishment to the soul, without straining it,' and is a 'handmaid of religion and philosophy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Playwrights should use the stage to present virtue and vice 'thoroughly displayed in a truthful and popular way' so audiences learn moral lessons without overt didacticism. Example: portrayals like Augustus and Cinna can inspire forgiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage supplements law and religion where they fail
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the influence of civil laws ends that of the stage begins; 'Where venality and corruption blind and bias justice ... the stage seizes the sword and scales.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic representation can expose crimes, hypocrisy, and overlooked virtues—use drama to unmask vice and to vindicate moral truths that institutions may neglect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of historical or literary exemplars to instruct public conscience
rubrics_metrics.description: The stage can revive 'great criminals of the past' as warnings and present exemplars of heroism or vice (e.g., Lear, Lady Macbeth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting historically or mythically resonant figures helps the stage educate and shape public sentiment. Anti-pattern: trivial or sensationalized portrayals that lack moral clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy (satire) often more effective than tragedy at correcting folly
rubrics_metrics.description: Mockery 'does the sting' that chastises pride and folly more effectively than hatred; 'the ludicrous is specially punished on the stage.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Playwrights aiming to reform manners should consider satire and comedy as powerful tools—audiences accept rebuke more readily when it is humorous than when it is purely moralizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage as practical school of civil wisdom and tolerance
rubrics_metrics.description: The stage 'teaches men to bear the strokes of fortune' and 'teaches us to be more considerate to the unfortunate, and to judge gently.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic works should portray motives and circumstances sympathetically so spectators can learn to withhold harsh judgement; use character context to cultivate humane responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: National/regional focus can build civic unity via the stage
rubrics_metrics.description: If poets 'selected well and from national topics' there would be a national stage that 'would have a great influence on the national temper and mind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Playwrights seeking cultural impact should draw on shared national subjects to unify audiences and promote civic identity; anti-pattern: purely cosmopolitan or disconnected material that fails to engage common concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage as superior, wholesome diversion countering destructive amusements
rubrics_metrics.description: The stage 'combines amusement with instruction' and prevents social degeneration into 'Bacchanal joys, gambling, follies.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic entertainment should be constructed to refresh and educate without numbing the mind; aim for pleasures that 'rouse noble passions' rather than merely titillate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic art's principal object: the pleasure of pity
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragic art 'proposes as its principal object the pleasure of pity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting tragedy, center the work on eliciting sympathetic pity in the spectator. This requires careful selection and arrangement of actions that awaken pity rather than mere horror or moral disgust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic pleasure arises from the exercise of reason and moral activity
rubrics_metrics.description: The pleasure we take in sad affections 'is from our moral nature' because 'this instinct of activity finds its gratification in them'—reason's free exercise produces aesthetic pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy should engage spectators' moral reasoning and sense of agency; design situations that allow contemplation of moral laws and the exercise of sympathy rather than only sensory shock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation of nature: choose actions that naturally awaken pity
rubrics_metrics.description: Art 'attains its end by the imitation of nature' and 'tragic art ought to imitate nature in those kinds of actions that are specially adapted to awaken pity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot and action should mirror plausible human causes and moral dilemmas that naturally elicit compassion. Anti-pattern: contrived or sensational events that do not plausibly produce pity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making the primary cause of misfortune morally inexcusable
rubrics_metrics.description: If the unhappy person's ruin is due to 'a personal and an inexcusable fault' or 'malicious will ... the pity we experience is diminished' and 'the supreme beauty of his work must always be seriously injured.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragic protagonists should not be solely culpable through vice or willful malice; sympathy is strongest when suffering is not the direct result of an inexcusable moral failing. Anti-patterns: villains masquerading as victims or catastrophes engineered by unrepentant wickedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catastrophe is more affecting when it follows overpowering circumstances or moral necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: When catastrophe comes 'through the imperious force of circumstances' or 'comes simply from the idea that a fellow-creature has been made to suffer,' pity is purer and more powerful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer tragic outcomes that spring from fate, conflicting duties, or unavoidable moral dilemmas rather than deliberate cruelty. Example: Corneille's The Cid—suffering that arises from honor vs. love.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between incongruity and higher consistency determines pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: In every tragic emotion 'there is an idea of incongruity' and 'it is the relation that these two opposite conceptions mutually bear which determines ... if the prevailing impression shall be pleasurable or the reverse.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should manage the vividness of incongruity versus the perception of consistency or higher purpose: if incongruity or the loss outweighs the gained end, the spectator may feel displeasure rather than pity. Craft plot so incongruity serves a deeper moral coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pity is heightened when the cause of suffering does not elicit indignation
rubrics_metrics.description: Pity increases when 'the cause of the misfortune ... has neither elicited our contempt nor our hatred' and when the cause 'has been brought against his inclination to become the cause of this misfortune.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray antagonists or causal agents with complexity or reluctant involvement to preserve audience sympathy for the victim. Avoid one-dimensional malicious antagonists who redirect emotional energy into indignation.
